concepts.name: Bank Rate: Definition and Structural Characteristics
key_dimensions: Legal basis under Section 49 of RBI Act, 1934 — statutory anchoring vs policy tool
No collateral/security requirement — distinguishing it from repo rate fundamentally
Long-term lending nature vs short-term overnight nature of repo
UPSC trap: Bank rate is NOT the same as MSF rate despite both being penal/signal rates

concepts.name: Repo Rate: Definition and Mechanism of Repurchase Agreement
key_dimensions: Collateralized borrowing — eligible securities (G-Secs, T-Bills) as collateral
Overnight/short-term nature and role in Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF)
Repurchase obligation — why it is a 'repo' and not a simple loan
UPSC trap: Repo is from bank's perspective borrowing, but from RBI's perspective it is injection of liquidity

concepts.name: Collateral Requirement: The Core Structural Difference
key_dimensions: Repo requires eligible collateral (G-Secs); bank rate requires none
Implications for credit risk on RBI's balance sheet
Why absence of collateral makes bank rate a 'last resort' signaling instrument
UPSC trap: MSF also requires collateral — often confused with bank rate

concepts.name: Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) and Repo Rate's Role Within It
key_dimensions: LAF corridor: MSF rate (ceiling) — Repo rate (policy rate) — Reverse repo rate (floor)
Repo rate as the operative policy rate since 2012 Urjit Patel Committee recommendations
Daily LAF operations vs bank rate's infrequent adjustment
UPSC trap: Bank rate is NOT part of LAF; it sits outside the LAF corridor

concepts.name: Interest Rate Relationship: Bank Rate, Repo Rate, MSF, and Reverse Repo
key_dimensions: Typical spread: Bank rate = MSF rate (both 25 bps above repo rate historically, but can differ)
Reverse repo rate = Repo rate minus 25 bps (the LAF floor)
When RBI changes repo rate, bank rate and MSF rate adjust automatically in tandem
UPSC trap: Bank rate and MSF rate are numerically equal in current RBI framework — candidates confuse them as identical instruments

concepts.name: Marginal Standing Facility (MSF): Overlap and Distinction with Bank Rate
key_dimensions: MSF introduced in 2011 as collateralized overnight borrowing above repo rate
MSF rate numerically equals bank rate but requires collateral; bank rate does not
Banks can borrow under MSF using SLR securities up to a defined percentage of NDTL
UPSC trap: Same rate but different instruments — MSF replaced bank rate's practical liquidity function

concepts.name: Transmission Mechanism: How Repo Rate Affects Economy vs Bank Rate
key_dimensions: Repo rate → short-term money market rates → lending/deposit rates → aggregate demand
Bank rate historically linked to penal interest on advances and rediscounting
Speed of transmission: Repo rate faster (daily operations); bank rate slower (signaling)
UPSC trap: India's monetary transmission is imperfect — external benchmark lending rate (EBLR) linkage to repo rate, not bank rate

concepts.name: External Benchmark Lending Rate (EBLR) and its Linkage to Repo Rate
key_dimensions: RBI mandated EBLR from October 2019 for retail and MSME loans
Repo rate as the most common external benchmark chosen by banks
MCLR regime vs EBLR regime — shift in rate transmission
UPSC trap: EBLR is linked to repo rate, NOT bank rate — a factual distinction frequently tested

concepts.name: Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) and Policy Rate Decision
key_dimensions: MPC decides repo rate (policy rate) under amended RBI Act Section 45ZB
Bank rate changes are a consequence of repo rate change — not separately decided by MPC
Six-member MPC: 3 RBI + 3 Government nominees; majority vote with RBI Governor casting vote
UPSC trap: MPC sets repo rate, not bank rate directly — bank rate adjustment is derivative

concepts.name: Historical Evolution: Bank Rate as Original Policy Rate to Repo Rate as Current Policy Rate
key_dimensions: Pre-1992: Bank rate was primary monetary policy instrument
Post-1991 reforms and introduction of LAF (2000): Repo rate became operative
Urjit Patel Committee (2014) formalized repo rate as the single policy rate
UPSC trap: Bank rate still exists legally but is no longer the operative monetary policy rate

concepts.name: Penal Rate Function: Bank Rate's Residual Role
key_dimensions: Bank rate used as reference for penal interest on CRR shortfall by banks
Penal interest on SLR shortfall also linked to bank rate
This residual regulatory function keeps bank rate relevant despite its reduced monetary role
UPSC trap: Candidates must know bank rate's current functional use is primarily penal/reference, not active liquidity management

concepts.name: Reverse Repo Rate: Absorption of Liquidity and Its Relationship to Repo Rate
key_dimensions: Reverse repo: RBI borrows from banks, absorbs excess liquidity from system
Always lower than repo rate — forms the floor of LAF corridor
During surplus liquidity (post-demonetization, COVID), reverse repo becomes effective policy rate
UPSC trap: When system liquidity is in surplus, reverse repo rate — not repo rate — is the binding rate

concepts.name: Open Market Operations (OMO) vs Repo: Liquidity Management Tools
key_dimensions: OMO: Outright purchase/sale of G-Secs — permanent liquidity injection/absorption
Repo: Temporary liquidity injection with repurchase agreement
Bank rate not a liquidity management tool — purely a rate signal and reference rate
UPSC trap: OMO affects money supply permanently; repo affects it temporarily — a classic comparison question

concepts.name: CRR and SLR: Relationship with Bank Rate and Repo Rate
key_dimensions: CRR maintained with RBI — no interest paid; shortfall penalized at bank rate
SLR maintained in approved securities — shortfall penalized linked to bank rate
Repo rate indirectly influences demand for CRR/SLR maintenance (opportunity cost)
UPSC trap: CRR shortfall penalty = bank rate + defined spread; candidates often misquote this

concepts.name: Inflation Targeting Framework and Repo Rate as its Instrument
key_dimensions: Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) adopted 2016 — CPI inflation target of 4% ± 2%
Repo rate is the instrument used to achieve inflation target
Bank rate plays no role in FIT framework — purely repo rate driven
UPSC trap: FIT framework operationalized through MPC and repo rate — not bank rate

concepts.name: Standing Deposit Facility (SDF): New Floor of LAF Corridor (2022)
key_dimensions: SDF introduced April 2022 as new floor, replacing reverse repo rate as operative floor
SDF: RBI absorbs liquidity without giving collateral to banks (uncollateralized absorption)
SDF rate = Repo rate minus 25 bps (same spread as earlier reverse repo)
UPSC trap: Post-2022, LAF corridor floor is SDF rate, NOT reverse repo rate — high-yield recent change

concepts.name: Impact of Repo Rate Change on Bond Yields and Government Borrowing Cost
key_dimensions: Repo rate hike → short-term rates rise → yield curve shifts upward → G-Sec yields rise
Higher G-Sec yields increase government's borrowing cost — fiscal-monetary interaction
Bank rate change has negligible direct impact on bond markets
UPSC trap: Relationship between monetary tightening (repo hike) and fiscal deficit financing cost

concepts.name: Quantitative vs Qualitative Monetary Policy Tools: Placing Repo and Bank Rate
key_dimensions: Repo rate and bank rate are quantitative (general) tools affecting overall credit
Qualitative tools: Selective Credit Control, moral suasion, margin requirements
CRR and SLR are also quantitative tools — candidates must map all tools correctly
UPSC trap: Bank rate is often misclassified as qualitative — it is a quantitative tool

concepts.name: Repo Rate During Crisis Management: COVID-19 and Demonetization Case Studies
key_dimensions: COVID-19: Emergency repo rate cuts (March 2020) — 75 bps cut outside MPC schedule
Reverse repo rate cut more than repo rate during COVID to discourage bank parking with RBI
Bank rate adjusted automatically alongside these repo rate movements
UPSC trap: Asymmetric adjustment of repo and reverse repo rates during COVID — deliberate policy to push banks to lend

concepts.name: Rediscounting of Bills: Bank Rate's Classical Function
key_dimensions: Bank rate classically = rate at which RBI rediscounts commercial bills/eligible securities from banks
This function has become largely theoretical in India's modern framework
Historically, rediscounting was primary refinance mechanism before LAF
UPSC trap: Textbooks still define bank rate through rediscounting — candidates must know it is now largely a signaling/penal rate
